Circadian PER2 Expression in Myopic vs Non-Myopic Chick Retina at ZT08

He Li | Master of Science in Computational Biology

2025-04-24

  • Introduction

Introduction

Circadian transcription factors coordinate photoreceptor renewal, neurotransmitter release, and ocular-growth signals in the retina (Iuvone et al., 2005).
PER2 peaks near mid-day in chick retina, modulates dopamine- and retinoic-acid pathways relevant to axial elongation, and its diurnal expression profile is shown to be altered during form-deprivation myopia progression (Stone et al., 2020, 2024).

In this project, I hypothesize that PER2 transcript levels differ between occluded (myopic) and untreated retinas at Zeitgeber Time 08 (ZT08) for females chicks using publicly available RNA-seq data (SRA SRP494275, HiSeq 4000, 2024-03-09). I analyze these libraries with a reproducible DESeq2 pipeline that emphasizes quality control and report whether a ZT08 snapshot suffices to reveal circadian dysregulation associated with experimental myopia.

Result

Differential-Expression Analyses

The DEA figure above shows the normalized counts for PER2 at ZT08 in normal eyes is approximately 1180, whereas myopic samples clustered around a median of 1045, yielding a non‐significant p-value of 0.325. Thus, at this single mid-day time point we do not have enough evidence to conclude a significant change in PER2 expression associated with myopia induction. This result implies that PER2 dysregulation in form-deprived eyes might be too subtle to capture at ZT08 alone or that circadian mis‐timing in myopia may manifest at other phases of the circadian cycle, underscoring the need for a full time‐course or larger sample size to resolve these dynamics.

Methods

Data

Run Accession Tissue Time (ZT) Condition
SRR28279786 Retina 08 Open
SRR28279788 Retina 08 Occluded
SRR28279790 Retina 08 Open
SRR28279792 Retina 08 Occluded

Data are from SRA study SRP494275 (BioProject PRJNA1086001) generated on 2024-03-09 by the New England College of Optometry using an Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. The libraries were constructed using the Illumina TruSeq Stranded mRNA kit, which incorporates a poly(A)‐selection step, resulting in 2 × 150 bp paired‐end reads. The samples above are used. The samples are downloaded using fastq-dump, then renamed and unzipped.

Raw-read quality assessment

The sequencing output for the four SRR runs was first inspected with FastQC.

Figure 1: Per‐base quality scores across all samples

The FastQC report for all four libraries shows consistently high per-base quality: median Phred scores remain above thirty (Q ≥ 30) from base 1 through the read tail, with no visible drop-off or nucleotide-specific spikes.

Figure 2: Adapter Content

Over-represented sequence analysis flagged a single Illumina TruSeq adapter fragment present in ~6 % of reads at the 3′ end of one sample; however, trimming is not needed because STAR’s soft-clipping automatically discards residual adapter during alignment. Our post-alignment QC confirmed a high unique mapping with low mismatch rates—I opted to forgo an additional trimming step. Skipping adapter removal avoids unnecessary length loss, maintains paired-read synchrony, and preserves maximal sequence complexity for downstream transcript-level quantification.

Figure 3: Alignment Scores

All four samples exhibit very similar STAR alignment profiles: about 85% of reads map uniquely to the Gallus gallus reference, < 5 % align to multiple loci, and the unmapped fraction remains below 10 %. Such high unique-mapping rates, with little multimapping or dropout, indicate well-complexed sample and accurate genome indexing.

Figure 4: Feature Counts

The featureCounts summary consolidates this result: roughly 75–80 % of aligned fragments are confidently assigned to annotated genes, while reads that fall outside annotated features or are deemed ambiguous or multimapped account for only 15–20 %. Crucially, the relative proportions are consistent across the two Open-eye and two Occluded-eye samples, confirming uniform data quality with not much technical bias or biological variations, excluding them as confounders in downstream differential-expression analyses.

Figure 5: Counts Normalization

The counts are mostly consistent across samples. A sample-wise normalization is conducted but the effect is minimal.

Figure 6: Variance vs. Mean (normalized counts)

The normalized counts show a slight variance-mean dependency, so I applied DESeq2’s Variance Stabilizing Transformation to remove that dependence. By stabilizing variance, VST ensures that low-count genes do not dominate Euclidean‐distance–based analyses in PCA and heatmap.

Figure 7: PCA and Heatmap

The PCA and Pearson correlation heatmap reveal that our samples do not cluster by condition, and replicate agreement is weaker than expected. Both shows no clear separation of OcclEye vs. OpenEye, with poor replicate concordance and lack of biological clustering.

Discussion

The study was constrained by a very small sample size (n = 2 per condition), which limited statistical power and precluded clear clustering of OpenEye versus OcclEye samples in both PCA and correlation analyses. Consequently, the differential expression analysis for PER2 at ZT08 did not reach significance (p = 0.479). Another limitation is that the chosen reference genome (GRCg7b) is not yet supported in IGV, restricting our ability to inspect read alignments for strand‐specific artifacts or novel splice variants. Future work should expand sampling and leverage an IGV‐compatible annotation to validate and visualize strandness and transcript structure in candidate genes.
